claim: Two male monkeys (Macaca mulatta; monkey T [15 years old] and monkey A [14 years old]) participated in this study.
source: Two male monkeys (Macaca mulatta; monkey T [15 years old] and monkey A [14 years old]) participated in this study.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the subjects used in the study.

claim: Both monkeys were used in a previous study of auditory cortex (Tsunada et al., 2016).
source: Both were used in a previous study of auditory cortex (Tsunada et al., 2016), and monkey T was also used in a previous study of vlPFC (Tsunada et al., 2011a).
evidence: Citation to previous work indicating prior use of these subjects.

claim: Monkey T was also used in a previous study of vlPFC (Tsunada et al., 2011a).
source: Both were used in a previous study of auditory cortex (Tsunada et al., 2016), and monkey T was also used in a previous study of vlPFC (Tsunada et al., 2011a).
evidence: Citation to previous work indicating prior use of this subject.

claim: The behavioral and neuronal data presented here have not been reported previously.
source: These monkeys participated in our previous study (Tsunada et al., 2016), but the behavioral and neuronal data presented here have not been reported previously.
evidence: Direct statement about the novelty of the data presented.

claim: Both monkeys' choice accuracy and RTs depended systematically on stimulus coherence.
source: Both monkeys' choice accuracy and RTs depended systematically on stimulus coherence (monkey T: n = 29 behavioral sessions; monkey A: n = 39 behavioral sessions; Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Behavioral measurements showing relationship between stimulus coherence and performance metrics, with reference to Figure 2a,b.

claim: For high-coherence stimuli, both monkeys almost always reported the correct answer with relatively short RTs.
source: For high-coherence stimuli, both monkeys almost always reported the correct answer with relatively short RTs.
evidence: Behavioral observation from the experimental data.

claim: As absolute coherence decreased, performance accuracy decreased and RT increased.
source: As absolute coherence decreased, performance accuracy decreased and RT increased.
evidence: Behavioral observation from the experimental data.

claim: Psychometric (choice) and chronometric (RT) data were well described jointly by a drift-diffusion model (DDM).
source: These psychometric (choice) and chronometric (RT) data were well described jointly by a drift-diffusion model (DDM; Figure 2a,b, pink lines; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008).
evidence: Model fitting results with citations to the DDM framework.

claim: The DDM fits provided a consistently good match to the data (average deviance was 11.82 for monkey T [χ2 -cumulative distribution, p<0.001] and 10.99 for monkey A [p<0.001]).
source: These fits provided a consistently good match to the data (average deviance was 11.82 for monkey T [χ2 -cumulative distribution, p<0.001] and 10.99 for monkey A [p<0.001]; Wichmann and Hill, 2001).
evidence: Statistical test results showing goodness of fit for the DDM model.

claim: The monkeys had consistent decision strategies, which were independent of the slight session-by-session differences in the choice of low- and high-frequency stimuli.
source: This result indicates that the monkeys had consistent decision strategies, which were independent of the slight session-by-session differences in the choice of low- and high-frequency stimuli.
evidence: Inference from the DDM fitting results about behavioral consistency.

claim: Monkey T tended to use a 'win-stay, lose-switch' strategy.
source: Monkey T tended to use a 'win-stay, lose-switch' strategy (top panels in Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Behavioral analysis showing sequential choice patterns with reference to Figure 2c,d.

claim: Monkey T tended to repeat the previous choice if that choice was rewarded but switched choices if the previous choice was not rewarded.
source: That is, this monkey tended to repeat the previous choice if that choice was rewarded but switched choices if the previous choice was not rewarded.
evidence: Behavioral observation describing the win-stay, lose-switch strategy.

claim: Monkey T's win-stay, lose-switch tendency was seen as stay-switch biases with positive values following rewarded trials and negative values following non-rewarded trials for both the pooled data (logistic regression: β0 [high/low bias]=−0.46, p<0.01; β1 [stimulus coherence]=2.50, p<0.01; β2 [stay/switch bias given that the previous trial was rewarded]=0.14, p<0.01; β3 [stay/switch bias given that the previous trial was not rewarded]=−0.30, p<0.01).
source: This tendency was seen as stay-switch biases with positive values following rewarded trials and negative values following non-rewarded trials for both the pooled data (Figure 2c; logistic regression: β0 [high/low bias]=−0.46, p<0.01; β1 [stimulus coherence]=2.50, p<0.01; β2 [stay/switch bias given that the previous trial was rewarded]=0.14, p<0.01; β3 [stay/switch bias given that the previous trial was not rewarded]=−0.30, p<0.01)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data showing sequential effects.

claim: Monkey T's win-stay, lose-switch tendency was seen in session-by-session data (median β0 = −0.50, Wilcoxon sign-rank test, p=0.04; β1 = 3.73, p<0.01; β2 = 0.27, p<0.01; β3 = −0.39, p=0.03).
source: and for the session-by-session data (Figure 2d; median β0 = −0.50, Wilcoxon sign-rank test, p=0.04; β1 = 3.73, p<0.01; β2 = 0.27, p<0.01; β3 = −0.39, p=0.03).
evidence: Statistical analysis of session-by-session behavioral data.

claim: Monkey A tended to use a 'win-switch' strategy.
source: In contrast, monkey A tended to use a 'win-switch' strategy (bottom panels in Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Behavioral analysis showing sequential choice patterns with reference to Figure 2c,d.

claim: Monkey A tended to switch choices following a rewarded choice.
source: That is, this monkey tended to switch choices following a rewarded choice.
evidence: Behavioral observation describing the win-switch strategy.

claim: Monkey A's win-switch strategy was evident in the pooled data (β0 = −0.45, p<0.01; β1 = 3.16, p<0.01; β2 = −0.19, p<0.01; β3 = −0.02, p=0.88).
source: Once again, this result was evident in both the pooled data (Figure 2c, β0 = −0.45, p<0.01; β1 = 3.16, p<0.01; β2 = −0.19, p<0.01; β3 = −0.02, p=0.88)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data showing sequential effects.

claim: Monkey A's win-switch strategy was evident in the session-by-session data (β0 = 0.50, p<0.01; β1 = 3.63, p<0.01; β2 = −0.19, p<0.01; β3 = 0.17, p=0.63).
source: and in the session-by-session data (Figure 2d, β0 = 0.50, p<0.01; β1 = 3.63, p<0.01; β2 = −0.19, p<0.01; β3 = 0.17, p=0.63).
evidence: Statistical analysis of session-by-session behavioral data.

claim: For both monkeys, we could not identify similar systematic effects on sequential RTs.
source: For both monkeys, we could not identify similar systematic effects on sequential RTs.
evidence: Negative result from behavioral analysis.

claim: Individual vlPFC neurons had task-driven activity that was modulated selectively by the monkeys' low- versus high-frequency choices.
source: Individual vlPFC neurons had task-driven activity that was modulated selectively by the monkeys' low- versus high-frequency choices (single-unit examples are shown in Figure 3 and summary population data are shown in Figure 4).
evidence: Neuronal recording data showing choice selectivity with references to Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The onset of choice selectivity for individual neurons spanned the time from the inferred decision commitment through the motor response (joystick movement) and to the time when the reward was delivered or withheld.
source: Across the population of recorded neurons, the onset of choice selectivity for individual neurons (which were recorded in separate sessions and across the two monkeys) spanned the time from the inferred decision commitment through the motor response (joystick movement) and to the time when the reward was delivered or withheld.
evidence: Temporal analysis of neuronal selectivity across the population.

claim: 13 and 15 high-frequency (ipsilateral)-preferring neurons were identified in monkeys T and A, respectively.
source: We identified 13 and 15 high-frequency (ipsilateral)-preferring neurons in monkeys T and A, respectively; and 10 and 14 low-frequency (contralateral)-preferring neurons, respectively
evidence: Count of neurons with specific choice preferences from recordings.

claim: 10 and 14 low-frequency (contralateral)-preferring neurons were identified in monkeys T and A, respectively.
source: We identified 13 and 15 high-frequency (ipsilateral)-preferring neurons in monkeys T and A, respectively; and 10 and 14 low-frequency (contralateral)-preferring neurons, respectively
evidence: Count of neurons with specific choice preferences from recordings.

claim: There was not any evidence for laterality in choice preference (χ2-test for H0: no difference in the proportion of contralateral- and ipsilateral preferring neurons, p>0.05 for both monkeys).
source: (there was not any evidence for laterality: χ2-test for H0: no difference in the proportion of contralateral- and ipsilateral preferring neurons, p>0.05 for both monkeys).
evidence: Statistical test showing no hemispheric bias in neuronal preferences.

claim: The choice selectivity of individual neurons was affected by the outcome of the current trial.
source: The choice selectivity of individual neurons was also affected by the outcome of the current trial.
evidence: Neuronal analysis showing modulation by trial outcome.

claim: Choice selectivity tended to be higher on correct trials than on error trials.
source: Specifically, choice selectivity tended to be higher on correct trials than on error trials (Figure 5).
evidence: Neuronal analysis comparing selectivity across trial outcomes with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The difference in choice selectivity between correct and error trials was apparent even before reward delivery.
source: This difference in choice selectivity was apparent even before reward delivery and thus could not be explained trivially as a direct response to reward delivery.
evidence: Temporal analysis of neuronal selectivity relative to reward timing.

claim: The difference in choice selectivity between correct and error trials likely reflected differences in decision processing on correct versus error trials, including more uncertainty in the neuronal representation of the sensory evidence and therefore possibly lower reward expectations on error trials.
source: Instead, this difference likely reflected differences in decision processing on correct versus error trials, including more uncertainty in the neuronal representation of the sensory evidence and therefore possibly lower reward expectations on error trials (Gold and Shadlen, 2003).
evidence: Interpretation of neuronal data with citation to theoretical framework.

claim: The responses of individual vlPFC neurons were not selective for stimulus coherence.
source: In contrast to these single-neuron modulations by choice and outcome, the responses of individual vlPFC neurons were not selective for stimulus coherence.
evidence: Negative result from single-neuron analysis.

claim: At any given time point, at most six vlPFC neurons were modulated by stimulus coherence for either preferred or non-preferred choices, which is not more than would be expected by chance.
source: In particular, we found that, at any given time point, at most six vlPFC neurons were modulated by stimulus coherence for either preferred or non-preferred choices, which is not more than would be expected by chance in our sample (Figure 4b).
evidence: Statistical analysis of coherence selectivity across the population with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: A more robust representation of stimulus coherence was found at the level of population neuronal activity.
source: However, we found a more robust representation of stimulus coherence at the level of population neuronal activity.
evidence: Population-level analysis showing coherence representation.

claim: The fraction of neurons with choice selectivity was systematically smaller with decreasing coherence.
source: The intuition for this discrepancy can be seen in Figure 4a: the fraction of neurons with choice selectivity was systematically smaller with decreasing coherence, implying that population-level signals were dependent on coherence.
evidence: Population analysis with reference to Figure 4a showing coherence-dependent effects.

claim: There was enough information across the population of 103 neurons for a linear classifier to decode both stimulus coherence and choice.
source: Although these effects did not correspond to statistically reliable differences in single-neuron coherence selectivity, there was enough information across the population of 103 neurons recorded from all sessions from both monkeys for a linear classifier to decode both stimulus coherence and choice (Figure 6).
evidence: Linear classifier analysis results with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Decoding accuracy for both coherence and choice rose above chance levels only after the end of the decision process.
source: In both cases, decoding accuracy rose above chance levels only after the end of the decision process (blue vertical stripes in the stimulus-aligned plots in the left panels of Figure 6)
evidence: Temporal analysis of decoding performance with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Decoding accuracy for both coherence and choice peaked around the time reward delivery.
source: and peaked around the time reward delivery, implying a form of post-decision processing.
evidence: Temporal analysis of decoding performance with interpretation.

claim: The vlPFC population had access to the key features of the decision process, including the strength of the evidence used to form the decision, the choice, and whether the choice was correct or an error.
source: Thus, the vlPFC population had access to the key features of the decision process, including the strength of the evidence used to form the decision, the choice, and whether the choice was correct or an error.
evidence: Summary of neuronal findings about decision-related information.

claim: These signals were not apparent before the decision commitment, implying that they did not contribute to the formation of the current decision.
source: These signals were not apparent before the decision commitment, implying that they did not contribute to the formation of the current decision.
evidence: Temporal analysis of neuronal signals with interpretation about their functional role.

claim: The timing of these signals suggests that they may play a role in post-decision processing that can link one decision to the next decision.
source: Instead, the timing of these signals suggests that they may play a role in post-decision processing that can link one decision to the next decision.
evidence: Interpretation of temporal patterns of neuronal activity.

claim: Neuronal activity in the post-decision epoch was selective for both the current choice and the subsequent choice.
source: Neuronal activity in the post-decision epoch was selective for both the current choice and the subsequent choice.
evidence: Neuronal analysis showing selectivity for sequential choices.

claim: Selectivity for the subsequent choice matched each monkey's idiosyncratic choice biases, particularly following rewarded trials.
source: This selectivity for the subsequent choice also matched each monkey's idiosyncratic choice biases (Figure 2c,d), particularly following rewarded trials.
evidence: Neuronal analysis showing correspondence with behavioral patterns.

claim: Monkey T's tendency to repeat rewarded trials was reflected in post-decision neuronal responses that tended to be slightly larger on trials in which the subsequent choice matched the neuron's choice selectivity.
source: Specifically, monkey T's tendency to repeat rewarded trials was reflected in post-decision neuronal responses that tended to be slightly larger on trials in which the subsequent choice matched the neuron's choice selectivity (Figure 7 top).
evidence: Neuronal analysis showing relationship between activity and subsequent behavior with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Monkey A's tendency to switch after rewarded trials was reflected in neuronal responses that tended to be slightly smaller on trials in which the subsequent choice matched the neuron's choice selectivity.
source: In contrast, monkey A's tendency to switch after rewarded trials was reflected in neuronal responses that tended, on average, to be slightly smaller on trials in which the subsequent choice matched the neuron's choice selectivity (Figure 7 bottom).
evidence: Neuronal analysis showing relationship between activity and subsequent behavior with reference to Figure 7.

claim: These effects had slightly different time courses in the two monkeys.
source: These effects had slightly different time courses in the two monkeys.
evidence: Temporal comparison of neuronal effects between subjects.

claim: In both monkeys, these effects occurred after the decision commitment on correct trials.
source: Nonetheless, in both cases, these effects occurred after the decision commitment on correct trials, which corresponds to a time period when evaluative processing could be used to adjust subsequent decisions.
evidence: Temporal analysis of neuronal effects with interpretation.

claim: We could not identify similarly reliable effects following error trials, possibly reflecting the much smaller data sets from those trials.
source: We could not identify similarly reliable effects following error trials, possibly reflecting the much smaller data sets from those trials.
evidence: Negative result with possible explanation.

claim: Microstimulation was applied from the time of stimulus onset until just after the behavioral response on a randomly selected 50% of trials in a subset of sessions (n = 11 sessions for monkey T, 21 sessions for monkey A).
source: We applied microstimulation from the time of stimulus onset until just after the behavioral response on a randomly selected 50% of trials in a subset of sessions (n = 11 sessions for monkey T, 21 sessions for monkey A).
evidence: Description of experimental manipulation protocol.

claim: Microstimulation did not systematically affect either the choice bias or the sensitivity of the decision on the current trial.
source: Despite the fact that this protocol was designed to test our initial hypothesis that vlPFC activity encoded formation of the current decision (and thus microstimulation was applied primarily during decision formation), we found that microstimulation did not systematically affect either the choice bias or the sensitivity of the decision on the current trial (single-site examples are shown in Figure 8a,b; population summaries are shown in Figure 8c,d).
evidence: Microstimulation results showing no effect on current trial with references to Figure 8.

claim: Microstimulation induced choice biases for the subsequent decision that depended systematically on the choice selectivity of the recorded vlPFC neuron at the microstimulation site.
source: Instead, we found that microstimulation induced choice biases for the subsequent decision that depended systematically on the choice selectivity of the recorded vlPFC neuron at the microstimulation site.
evidence: Microstimulation results showing effects on subsequent trial.

claim: If microstimulation was applied at a site that was tuned for low-frequency choices, it tended to cause a low-choice bias on the subsequent trial.
source: If microstimulation was applied at a site that was tuned for low-frequency choices, it tended to cause a low-choice bias on the subsequent trial (single-site example in Figure 8e).
evidence: Microstimulation result with reference to Figure 8e.

claim: If microstimulation was applied at a site that was tuned for high-frequency choices, it tended to cause a high-choice bias on the subsequent trial.
source: In contrast, if microstimulation was applied at a site that was tuned for high-frequency choices, it tended to cause a high-choice bias on the subsequent trial (single-site example in Figure 8f).
evidence: Microstimulation result with reference to Figure 8f.

claim: Across the population of microstimulation sites from both monkeys, the induced choice bias on the subsequent trial was correlated positively with the strength and direction of choice selectivity at the given site.
source: Accordingly, across the population of microstimulation sites from both monkeys, the induced choice bias on the subsequent trial was correlated positively with the strength and direction of choice selectivity at the given site (Figure 8g).
evidence: Population-level microstimulation analysis with reference to Figure 8g.

claim: Microstimulation at a site with neuronal activity that was selective for a low- or high-frequency choice on the current trial biased the monkeys' choices toward a low- or high-frequency choice, respectively, on the subsequent trial.
source: In other words, microstimulation at a site with neuronal activity that was selective for a low- or high-frequency choice on the current trial biased the monkeys' choices toward a low- or high-frequency choice, respectively, on the subsequent trial.
evidence: Summary of microstimulation effects.

claim: The absolute magnitude of the microstimulation-induced bias was positively correlated with the strength of choice selectivity at the site of microstimulation.
source: Further, the absolute magnitude of this bias was positively correlated with the strength of choice selectivity at the site of microstimulation.
evidence: Quantitative relationship between neuronal selectivity and microstimulation effect.

claim: We did not identify any concomitant, systematic changes in psychometric sensitivity from microstimulation.
source: We did not identify any concomitant, systematic changes in psychometric sensitivity (Figure 8h).
evidence: Negative result from microstimulation analysis with reference to Figure 8h.

claim: Microstimulation effects depended on specific choice patterns, albeit slightly differently for the two monkeys.
source: These microstimulation effects also depended on specific choice patterns, albeit slightly differently for the two monkeys.
evidence: Analysis of microstimulation effects conditional on behavioral patterns.

claim: When microstimulation was applied on a trial that resulted in a rewarded high choice, the subsequent choice tended to be biased in the same direction as the choice selectivity of the neuron recorded at the site of microstimulation for both monkeys (monkey T: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient ρ = 0.90, p<0.001; monkey A: ρ = 0.61, p=0.04).
source: When microstimulation was applied on a trial that resulted in a rewarded high choice, the subsequent choice tended to be biased in the same direction as the choice selectivity of the neuron recorded at the site of microstimulation for both monkeys (monkey T: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient ρ = 0.90, p<0.001; monkey A: ρ = 0.61, p=0.04).
evidence: Statistical analysis of conditional microstimulation effects.

claim: When microstimulation was applied on a trial that resulted in a rewarded low choice, a similar effect was found only for one of the two monkeys (monkey T: ρ = 0.91, p<0.001; monkey A: ρ = 0.10, p=0.75).
source: When microstimulation was applied on a trial that resulted in a rewarded low choice, a similar effect was found only for one of the two monkeys (monkey T: ρ = 0.91, p<0.001; monkey A: ρ = 0.10, p=0.75).
evidence: Statistical analysis of conditional microstimulation effects showing subject-specific differences.

claim: These microstimulation effects are consistent with the hypothesis that vlPFC activity is causally involved in evaluative processing that adjusts subsequent decisions.
source: Together, these effects are consistent with the hypothesis that vlPFC activity is causally involved in evaluative processing that adjusts subsequent decisions.
evidence: Interpretation of microstimulation results.

claim: vlPFC population activity had many of the hallmarks of a decision variable that could account for the monkeys' patterns of choices and RTs, including selectivity for the strength of the sensory evidence, the monkey's choice, and whether the choice was correct or incorrect.
source: vlPFC population activity had many of the hallmarks of a decision variable that could account for the monkeys' patterns of choices and RTs, including selectivity for the strength of the sensory evidence, the monkey's choice, and whether the choice was correct or incorrect.
evidence: Summary of neuronal findings about decision-related signals.

claim: These forms of selectivity were not evident until after the time of the decision commitment and thus were inconsistent with a role for these neurons in forming the current decision.
source: However, these forms of selectivity were not evident until after the time of the decision commitment and thus were inconsistent with a role for these neurons in forming the current decision.
evidence: Temporal analysis of neuronal selectivity with interpretation about functional role.

claim: Post-decision selectivity appeared to support sequential adjustments to the decision process.
source: Instead, this post-decision selectivity appeared to support sequential adjustments to the decision process.
evidence: Interpretation of neuronal findings in relation to behavior.

claim: Post-decision neuronal activity was modulated by each monkey's idiosyncratic sequential choice biases.
source: Specifically, post-decision neuronal activity was modulated by each monkey's idiosyncratic sequential choice biases.
evidence: Neuronal analysis showing relationship with behavioral patterns.

claim: Electrical microstimulation at vlPFC sites affected the monkeys' choices on the subsequent, but not the current, trial.
source: Further, electrical microstimulation at vlPFC sites affected the monkeys' choices on the subsequent, but not the current, trial.
evidence: Summary of microstimulation results.

claim: These results imply a role for post-decision vlPFC activity in encoding information about the process of forming the just-completed decision that is used to generate individualized biases that affect the subsequent decision.
source: Together, these results imply a role for post-decision vlPFC activity in encoding information about the process of forming the just-completed decision that is used to generate individualized biases that affect the subsequent decision.
evidence: Overall interpretation of combined neuronal and microstimulation findings.

claim: Post-decision signals are a form of 'decision-trace' activity that has been identified in numerous brain areas, including parts of the prefrontal and parietal cortices.
source: These post-decision signals are a form of 'decision-trace' activity that has been identified in numerous brain areas, including parts of the prefrontal and parietal cortices (Barraclough et al., 2004; Bizzi, 1968; Funahashi et al., 1991; Tsujimoto and Sawaguchi, 2004; Ding and Gold, 2012a; Hwang et al., 2017; Akrami et al., 2018; Ding and Gold, 2010; Histed et al., 2009).
evidence: Contextualization of findings with citations to related work.

claim: Decision-trace activity represents information about the immediately preceding decision that can be used as part of a feedback-driven learning process to adjust future decisions based on a comparison between the expected and actual outcome of prior decisions.
source: This kind of activity represents information about the immediately preceding decision that can be used as part of a feedback-driven learning process to adjust future decisions based on a comparison between the expected and actual outcome of prior decisions (Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation with citation to learning framework.

claim: The population-level post-decision representations identified in the vlPFC are, in principle, sufficient to compute a confidence or reward-expectation signal for the just-completed decision.
source: Consistent with this idea, the population-level post-decision representations that we identified in the vlPFC are, in principle, sufficient to compute a confidence or reward-expectation signal for the just-completed decision (Ding and Gold, 2010; Ding and Gold, 2012a; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Kepecs et al., 2008).
evidence: Interpretation of findings with citations to related theoretical work.

claim: This confidence signal could be compared to the actual outcome to adjust the subsequent decision, possibly in other cortical or subcortical brain regions known to encode reward feedback and prediction error.
source: This signal could then be compared to the actual outcome to adjust the subsequent decision, possibly in other cortical or subcortical brain regions known to encode reward feedback and prediction error (Schultz, 2015).
evidence: Speculation about broader circuit mechanisms with citation.

claim: The fact that the two monkeys used different biasing strategies (win-stay for monkey T, win-switch for monkey A) affects the interpretation of the findings in two primary ways.
source: The fact that our two monkeys used different biasing strategies (win-stay for monkey T, win-switch for monkey A) affects the interpretation of our findings in two primary ways.
evidence: Discussion of how subject-specific differences inform interpretation.

claim: vlPFC selectivity for the subsequent choice was consistent with each monkey's strategy, which provides stronger support for the behavioral relevance of these signals than if they encoded features of behavior that were only present on average.
source: First, vlPFC selectivity for the subsequent choice was consistent with each monkey's strategy. This result provides stronger support for the behavioral relevance of these signals than if they encoded features of behavior that were only present on average.
evidence: Interpretation of how subject-specific correspondence strengthens conclusions.

claim: Microstimulation effects on the subsequent choice tended to depend on the choice tuning of neurons at the site of microstimulation and not the idiosyncratic sequential bias strategy of the monkey.
source: Second, our microstimulation effects on the subsequent choice tended to depend on the choice tuning of neurons at the site of microstimulation and not the idiosyncratic sequential bias strategy of the monkey.
evidence: Summary of microstimulation findings in relation to subject-specific strategies.

claim: The vlPFC provides a choice-dependent signal that is used to generate sequential biases but may not participate directly in forming the idiosyncratic strategies that use those biases.
source: This result implies that the vlPFC provides a choice-dependent signal that is used to generate sequential biases but may not participate directly in forming the idiosyncratic strategies that use those biases.
evidence: Interpretation of microstimulation results about functional role.

claim: These findings are broadly consistent with recent studies that have shown a role for the vlPFC in strategy-switching and probabilistic-learning tasks, which share features of the sequential effects identified.
source: These findings are broadly consistent with recent studies that have shown a role for the vlPFC in strategy-switching and probabilistic-learning tasks, which share features of the sequential effects that we identified (Baxter et al., 2009; Rudebeck et al., 2017).
evidence: Contextualization with citations to related work.

claim: The findings of primarily post-decision processing in the vlPFC are somewhat inconsistent with other studies that have implicated the PFC in forming auditory and other decisions.
source: However, our findings of primarily post-decision processing in the vlPFC are somewhat inconsistent with other studies that have implicated the PFC in forming auditory and other decisions (Russ et al., 2008b; Cohen et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Bizley and Cohen, 2013; Kim and Shadlen, 1999).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature with citations.

claim: The reasons for the discrepancy with other studies are not clear.
source: The reasons for this discrepancy are not clear.
evidence: Acknowledgment of uncertainty about differences with prior work.

claim: One possible reason for the discrepancy is that a different PFC population was sampled than in other studies, and these different populations make different contributions to decision versus post-decision processing.
source: One possible reason is that we sampled a different PFC population than in these other studies, and these different populations make different contributions to decision versus post-decision processing.
evidence: Speculation about possible explanation for differences with prior work.

claim: Another possibility is that previous reports of decision-related activity were also largely post-decisional.
source: Another possibility is that previous reports of decision-related activity were also largely post-decisional.
evidence: Alternative speculation about interpretation of prior work.

claim: Accounting for the possibility that previous reports were post-decisional is not straightforward because the previous studies did not use RT tasks, making it difficult to interpret those results in terms of whether the reported decision-related signals occurred before or after the decision was formed on each trial.
source: However, accounting for this possibility is not straightforward: the previous studies did not use RT tasks, making it difficult to interpret those results in terms of whether the reported decision-related signals occurred before or after the decision was formed on each trial (Russ et al., 2008b; Cohen et al., 2009; Fritz et al., 2010).
evidence: Discussion of methodological differences with prior work with citations.

claim: We still do not know the brain regions that form the decision for our task and consequently do not understand the mechanisms underlying these decisions.
source: We still do not know the brain regions that form the decision for our task and consequently do not understand the mechanisms underlying these decisions.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitation of current study.

claim: Because the monkeys' choice and RT patterns reflected both the temporal accumulation of sensory evidence and sequential choice biases, we would expect the putative brain regions that form the decision to implement two key operations: temporally accumulate the sensory evidence represented in the auditory cortex and combine this accumulated evidence with historical sensory, outcome, and choice information to drive sequential choice biases.
source: Because the monkeys' choice and RT patterns reflected both the temporal accumulation of sensory evidence and sequential choice biases, we would expect these putative brain regions to implement two key operations. First, they should temporally accumulate the sensory evidence that is represented in the auditory cortex, particularly AL (Tsunada et al., 2016). Second, they should combine this accumulated evidence with historical sensory, outcome, and choice information, similar to that represented in vlPFC, to drive sequential choice biases (Ding and Gold, 2012a; Ding and Gold, 2010; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Hwang et al., 2017; Akrami et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation about expected properties of decision-forming regions with citations.

claim: One possibility for brain regions that form the decision is a set of other brain areas that have shown information-accumulation activity on other tasks, such as the dorsolateral PFC and parts of the posterior parietal cortex.
source: One possibility is a set of other brain areas that have shown information-accumulation activity on other tasks, such as the dorsolateral PFC and parts of the posterior parietal cortex (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Brody and Hanks, 2016).
evidence: Speculation about candidate brain regions with citations.

claim: The posterior parietal cortex is a particularly compelling target of future studies because in rodents, it contributes to history-dependent choice biases on an auditory decision task.
source: The posterior parietal cortex is a particularly compelling target of future studies because in rodents, it contributes to history-dependent choice biases on an auditory decision task (Akrami et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation about future research directions with citation to relevant work.

claim: Another intriguing possibility is an auditory-specific circuit involving the parabelt region of auditory cortex, which receives direct input from AL, projects to the vlPFC, and analyzes acoustic properties of behaviorally relevant sounds.
source: Another intriguing possibility is an auditory-specific circuit involving the parabelt region of auditory cortex, which receives direct input from AL, projects to the vlPFC, and analyzes acoustic properties of behaviorally relevant sounds (Hackett et al., 1999; Romanski et al., 1999; Petkov et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation about alternative candidate circuit with citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Future studies that aim to identify neuronal activity related to decision formation for this kind of auditory task will likely benefit from an RT design to better identify the temporal epoch of decision formation.

claim: The time course of these representations was distributed across the neuronal population: different neurons (recorded in separate sessions) responded selectively at relatively restricted times with onsets that tiled the task epoch.
source: The time course of these representations was also distributed across the neuronal population: different neurons (in our case, recorded in separate sessions) responded selectively at relatively restricted times with onsets that tiled the task epoch in a manner similar to other reports of working memory in the prefrontal cortex (Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006; Jun et al., 2010; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Brody et al., 2003; Schmitt et al., 2017).

claim: Microstimulation started with stimulus onset and terminated at joystick movement.
source: Microstimulation started with stimulus onset and terminated at joystick movement.

claim: The DDM models a decision process in which noisy evidence is accumulated over time until it reaches a fixed bound.
source: Psychophysical and chronometric data were fit to a standard drift-diffusion model (DDM), which models a decision process in which noisy evidence is accumulated over time until it reaches a fixed bound (Brunton et al., 2013; Ding and Gold, 2012a; Eckhoff et al., 2008; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Green et al., 2010; Mulder et al., 2013; Ratcliff et al., 1999; Shadlen et al., 2006).

source: This version of the model had five free parameters: k, A, B, F1, and F2.

claim: In the DDM, k governed the stimulus sensitivity of the moment-by-moment sensory evidence.
source: k governed the stimulus sensitivity of the moment-by-moment sensory evidence.
evidence: Description of model parameter.

claim: In the DDM, the decision variable was the temporal accumulation of momentary sensory evidence.
source: The decision variable was the temporal accumulation of this momentary sensory evidence.
evidence: Description of model component.

claim: In the DDM, a decision occurred when the decision variable reached a decision bound (+A or -B, which corresponded to a high- and low-frequency choice, respectively).
source: A decision occurred when this decision variable reached a decision bound (+A or -B, which corresponded to a high- and low-frequency choice, respectively).

source: 'Decision time' was the time between stimulus onset and the crossing of either bound.

source: Response time (RT; which was the time from stimulus onset to the onset of joystick movement) could also be defined as the sum of this decision time and a 'non-decision time' (F1 for a high-frequency choice and F2 for a low-frequency choice).

claim: Non-decision time includes processes such as stimulus encoding and motor preparation.
source: Non-decision time includes processes such as stimulus encoding and motor preparation.

claim: The time of 'decision commitment' was defined as the end of the decision time plus an additional 50 ms to account for sensory latency.

claim: To identify if and when each neuron had statistically significant choice-related activity, a running Wilcoxon rank-sum test was performed for each pair of stimulus coherence bins with the same magnitude but different signs (H0: firing rates elicited by the coherence pair are the same, p<0.05, FDR corrected).
source: To identify if and when each neuron had statistically significant choice-related activity, we performed a running Wilcoxon rank-sum test for each pair of stimulus coherence bins with the same magnitude but different signs (H0: firing rates elicited by the coherence pair are the same, p<0.05, FDR corrected; Ding and Gold, 2012a; Ding and Gold, 2010).

claim: Choice-related activity was analyzed in 300 ms time bins, shifted in 10 ms steps.
source: We analyzed choice-related activity in 300 ms time bins, shifted in 10 ms steps.

claim: Choice selectivity was quantified using an ROC analysis, which measures the ability of an ROC-based ideal observer to predict a monkey's choice based only on firing rates.
source: Choice selectivity was quantified using an ROC analysis, which measures the ability of an ROC-based ideal observer to predict a monkey's choice based only on firing rates (Russ et al., 2008b; Tsunada et al., 2016; Tsunada et al., 2011b).
evidence: Description of analysis method with citations.

claim: Linear classifiers were used to test whether vlPFC population activity was modulated by stimulus coherence or by behavioral choice.
source: We used linear classifiers (Meyers et al., 2008; Bishop, 2006) to test whether vlPFC population activity was modulated by stimulus coherence (using four binned ranges of coherence: [1] −100% – −50%, [2] −50 – 0%, [3] 0% – +50%, and [4]+50% – +100%) or by behavioral choice (high- versus low-frequency choices across all coherences).

claim: The classification analysis was restricted to data generated on correct trials only to help ensure that the effects of stimulus coherence and behavioral choice on vlPFC population activity could be quantified and not outcome effects.
source: This analysis was restricted to data generated on correct trials only to help to ensure that we could quantify the effects of stimulus coherence and behavioral choice on vlPFC population activity and not outcome effects (correct versus incorrect trials).
evidence: Justification for analysis design choice.

claim: For each classifier and for each neuron, firing rate was z-scored and trials were randomly subsampled so that there were equal numbers of trials for each condition.

source: Each classification analysis underwent a 10-fold cross-validation procedure to avoid overfitting.

claim: For the coherence classifier, a 'one-versus-all' classification was implemented in which four classifiers (one for each binned coherence range) were built and trained to discriminate between one particular coherence range versus all of the remaining three coherence ranges.

claim: For both classifiers, the fraction of times that the test data was classified correctly was calculated and average performance over 1000 different instantiations of a classifier was reported.
